entities.summary:
Japan is an island country in East Asia, an archipelago of 6,852 islands in the Pacific Ocean off the northeast coast of the Asian mainland, of which four main islands (Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu, Shikoku) constitute 97% of the land area. With 125 million people, Japan is the world's eleventh-most populous country and maintains the world's third-largest economy by GDP.

Japanese civilization has a continuous history of over 2,000 years. The Yayoi period (300 BCE – 300 CE) saw the introduction of wet-rice agriculture and bronze and iron technology. The Nara (710–784) and Heian (794–1185) periods produced Japan's classical literary and artistic culture, including The Tale of Genji (c. 1000 CE) — arguably the world's first novel. The feudal period (1185–1868) saw the rise of the samurai class, the Shogunate system, and centuries of internal warfare before Tokugawa unification (1600). The Meiji Restoration (1868) initiated Japan's rapid modernization — within 50 years it had defeated China (1895) and Russia (1905) and emerged as Asia's first modern imperial power.

Japan's military expansionism culminated in World War II's Pacific theater (1941–1945), ending with the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki (August 1945) and unconditional surrender. Post-war reconstruction produced the Japanese Economic Miracle (1950s–1990s) — the fastest sustained economic growth in history. Japan became the world's second-largest economy (1968–2010), a technological innovator in electronics, automobiles, and robotics. Its 1990 asset bubble collapse and subsequent 'Lost Decades' of stagnation became the paradigmatic case study of post-bubble economic deflation.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Japan's feudal period saw the rise of the samurai class, which had a significant impact on East Asian politics and culture. The country's classical literary and artistic culture, including The Tale of Genji, also influenced regional and global trends.
